events.name: A coffee chain opens on your block
events.text: A national chain takes the corner unit 150 meters away. Commuters who only want a fast cup now have a second door to choose from.
events.note: No controlled measurement exists for an independent cafe. Owners' accounts: one saw 10% of afternoon sales go when a Starbucks opened and won it back with breakfast sandwiches; a Hanover, New Hampshire cafe reported falling sales; in Minneapolis one neighbor lost coffee sales and another none. Between identical stores the measured effect is small: 1.2% per extra Starbucks within a mile (Marketing Science, 2018). 7% for six months is my planning value inside a 0-15% range.

events.name: The chain store down the block closes
events.text: The chain did not renew its lease. Its regulars need a new morning stop this week, and habits formed now tend to stay.
events.note: Center for an Urban Future, 2025 chain census: Starbucks closed 42 New York City stores in a year, more than any chain that stayed; chains as a whole fell 1.3% (112 stores), the sixth decline in eight years. The 6% gain for the nearest independent is my estimate.

events.name: A coffee cart sets up by the subway stairs
events.text: A licensed cart now sells drip coffee and a roll for about half your price, right where commuters come up from the train.
events.note: Intro 431, enacted over a veto in January 2026: 2,200 more mobile food vendor supervisory license applications each year from 2026 through 2031, on top of 6,880 existing food vendor permits. Carts work the warm months. 4% is my estimate: the cart takes drip coffee from commuters, not lattes from regulars.

events.name: January slump
events.text: New Year's resolutions, cold mornings and empty offices. Cafe owners say customers disappear at the start of every year.
events.note: Fresh Cup: coffee shop customers 'notoriously disappear at the beginning of every year'. Placer.ai: office visits stay low from Thanksgiving through the first weeks of January; the first and fourth quarters underperform. The 8% is extra.monthCurve's January value against an average month, my estimate.

events.name: Autumn drink season
events.text: The chains launch their autumn drinks in late August and customers go looking for something seasonal. Shops with a drink of their own share in it.
events.note: Placer.ai: Starbucks visits rose 3.4% in October and 14.7% in November 2021 month over month, its usual seasonal climb; visits ran 44.5% above average on the holiday drink launch day in November 2025. 3% for a neighborhood shop is my estimate, and it should apply only to shops that run the limited_time_drink lever.

events.name: Offices empty out for the holidays
events.text: From Thanksgiving week to the first days of January the office towers thin out. Morning lines shorten everywhere that lives on commuters.
events.note: Placer.ai: office visits in December 2025 were 33.1% under 2019, against 21.8% under in July 2025, and that was the busiest December since the pandemic. The 7% is for a mixed neighborhood block; an office-district shop loses far more (extra.eventCatalog holiday_office_exodus).

events.name: Summer Fridays
events.text: From late July to Labor Day the offices run half empty, most of all on Fridays. Residents are away too.
events.note: Placer.ai's August 2025 index: 'an end of summer slump'; Kastle card swipes dip in the week of July 4 and from late July to Labor Day. New York's Friday share of office visits was 11.9% in the first half of 2026. 4% for a mixed block is my estimate.

events.name: Peak visitor season
events.text: Hotels are full and the sidewalks are slow. Visitors find cafes on a map: the rating and the photos do the selling.
events.note: CoStar: New York City hotel occupancy led the 25 largest US markets at 87.9% in May 2025, 86.6% in September and 89.4% in October. New York had 65 million visitors in 2025 and forecasts 66.3 million for 2026. 5% for an average block is my estimate; tourist corridors gain more.

events.name: Delivery keeps growing
events.text: New Yorkers place more app orders every year, even with higher courier pay. A cafe that is not listed does not see those orders.
events.note: City report of October 21, 2026: 3.3 million app orders a week by June 2026, 700,000 more than in December 2023; consumer demand up 29% since 2023; the courier minimum is $22.13 an hour since April 1, 2026. 29% over about two and a half years is close to 10% a year; 8% is used.

events.name: Customers trade down
events.text: Households cut small luxuries first. Quick-service visits are falling across the country and a $7 latte is easy to skip.
events.note: Placer.ai: quick-service restaurant visits were 1.3% lower in the first seven months of 2026 than a year earlier, and 4.5% lower in May. Starbucks' US transactions fell 10% in its fourth fiscal quarter of 2024. 4% for an independent is my estimate between the two.

events.name: Campus summer break
events.text: Classes end in May and the students leave until September. The afternoon tables are suddenly free.
events.note: NYU's 2026-27 calendar: fall classes start September 2, 2026 and end December 14, exams December 16-22; spring classes start January 19, 2027. CUNY had about 247,000 students in fall 2025. 5% is my estimate for a mixed East Village block; a shop on the campus edge loses about 12% (the place model on the keen-cray branch).

events.name: World Cup summer
events.text: World Cup matches across the river and fans from everywhere in town. Shops that give them a reason to stop do well; a shop next to a closed street does not.
events.note: June 11 - July 19, 2026. Restaurant transactions in New York and New Jersey ran 18.5% higher during the group stage (trade roundup); venues that showed the matches reported 63% higher sales (NYC Hospitality Alliance survey); hotel room revenue rose 20.6%; one restaurant a five-minute walk from the stadium reported 60% lower sales on match days. 4% for an ordinary cafe is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: A 'B' goes up in your window
eventCatalog.text: The re-inspection ended with 14 to 27 points. The card stays until the next inspection cycle, and people do look.
eventCatalog.trigger: Follows from the player's own open violations: 14-27 points at re-inspection (extra.inspectionPoints)
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop's own inspection score in the city's open restaurant inspection data
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not found: the share of New York cafes holding a B was not read from the city's data in this session
eventCatalog.note: Rothbart, Schwartz and others (2019): an A raises revenue and lowers the chance of closing relative to a B. Size not seen; 5% is a planning value in a 2-10% range. 88% of New Yorkers say they consider the grade. Duration: the pack's own next-cycle window after a B, 150-210 days.

eventCatalog.name: A 'C' goes up in your window
eventCatalog.text: 28 points or more at re-inspection. Few people walk past a C and come in anyway.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop's own inspection score
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not found
eventCatalog.note: Same study: a C lowers revenue and raises the chance of closing relative to a B. 12% is a planning value. Duration: the pack's next-cycle window after a C, 90-150 days.

eventCatalog.name: Reopening after the Health Department closed you
eventCatalog.text: The yellow closure sticker was on the door for days and the listing sites noticed. Regulars come back slowly.
eventCatalog.trigger: Any violation that closed the shop (closureDays above zero)
eventCatalog.realSignal: Closures appear in the city's open inspection data and on the Health Department's restaurant lookup
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not found
eventCatalog.note: No measurement of sales after a closure was found. 15% for two months is a planning value, set above the C effect because a closure is public in more places than the window.

eventCatalog.name: Your rating slips under four stars
eventCatalog.text: On the map you are now the 3.9 between two 4.4s. Newcomers and tourists pick by that number.
eventCatalog.trigger: The shop's star rating (extra.mechanics star_rating) falls below 4.0
eventCatalog.realSignal: The rating shown on Google Maps and Yelp
eventCatalog.realFrequency: BrightLocal 2026: 68% of consumers want at least four stars before using a local business; 31% want four and a half, up from 17% a year earlier. In a 2026 sample of 570 restaurant profiles 14.9% were rated under 4.0 and the average was 4.27; 500 US cafe profiles averaged 4.26
eventCatalog.note: A threshold on top of the smooth star effect: the people who filter by four stars never see the shop. Regulars do not care, so the hit is on newcomers only: 5% of all orders is my estimate for a shop where about a third of orders come from people who do not know it yet.

eventCatalog.name: The rating rounds up half a star
eventCatalog.text: Your average crept from 4.2 to 4.3 and the site now shows four and a half stars. Nothing else changed.
eventCatalog.trigger: The average rating crosses a rounding line (x.25 or x.75) upward
eventCatalog.realSignal: The displayed, rounded rating on Yelp
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Anderson and Magruder, 2012: restaurants just above a rounding line sold out 19 percentage points (49%) more often than those just below
eventCatalog.note: Half of Luca's 5-9% per star is 2.5-4.5%; 4% is used. The same step down costs the same.

eventCatalog.name: The reviews start saying 'slow'
eventCatalog.text: For a month the morning line moved slower than people's patience. Now the newest reviews all mention the wait.
eventCatalog.trigger: More than 5% of a month's demand was lost for lack of staff or bar capacity
eventCatalog.realSignal: Share of the shop's recent reviews that mention waiting
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks' own count before its 2025 turnaround: only about half of orders were ready within four minutes
eventCatalog.note: The size is my estimate: a quarter of a star (0.06 on the reputation scale) for a month of visible waits. BrightLocal's 2026 survey stresses that recent reviews decide.

eventCatalog.name: Phone orders pile up at the handoff
eventCatalog.text: Twenty cups with stickers crowd the counter at 8:15. People in line watch them being made first, and some leave.
eventCatalog.trigger: Order-ahead runs with no cap while the rush hour is above 85% of bar capacity
eventCatalog.realSignal: Share of rush-hour orders placed ahead; Starbucks counted stores above 20%
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks, early 2017: 1,200 stores took 20% or more of rush orders by phone, up from 13 stores a year before
eventCatalog.note: Starbucks' chief operating officer named the congestion at the handoff as the biggest cause of a weak quarter: people saw the crowd and did not order. Sizes are my estimates. In 2025 the company answered with a queueing algorithm and capped pickup slots.

eventCatalog.name: A big price jump gets noticed
eventCatalog.text: You raised prices by more than 8% in one go. Regulars do the sum at the register and say so online.
eventCatalog.trigger: The price order rises more than 8% within one month
eventCatalog.realSignal: The shop's own price history against the drift of menu prices (Toast: about 4% a year)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Toast: the median drip coffee rose 4.3% in the year to February 2026 and the median cold brew 4.0% in the year to October 2026
eventCatalog.note: On top of the ordinary elasticity. Owners in 2025: 'You always get nervous when you raise prices... you may lose some, especially at first' (Indianapolis); in Colorado most customers understood and changed nothing. Trade advice is to move in small steps and say why. 3% for two months is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: The map says you are open, the door says you are not
eventCatalog.text: You changed your hours and the listing did not. A few people came to a locked door and wrote about it.
eventCatalog.trigger: The hours lever changed while the reviews lever is set to 'ignore'
eventCatalog.realSignal: Hours shown on the shop's map listings against real hours
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Not found. One turnaround story: a cafe's sales recovered within two months once people learned it was still open and it had a web presence
eventCatalog.note: Sizes are my estimates.

eventCatalog.name: A coffee chain opens within sight
eventCatalog.text: A national chain takes the corner unit. It will pull the commuters who only want a fast cup; your regulars are yours to keep.
eventCatalog.realSignal: New food service permits and storefront leases on the block; the chain counts of the Center for an Urban Future
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Dunkin' has 623 stores in the city (2025); Starbucks had 328 in 2024 and closed 42 in 2025; every block within reach of a subway stop already has one or expects one
eventCatalog.note: See events chain_opens_nearby. After six months the effect should fade to about -3%: the people who switched were the least attached.

eventCatalog.name: An app-only chain opens with $1.99 coffee
eventCatalog.text: A new chain two blocks away runs on an app and kiosks and hands every new user a $1.99 drink. Price shoppers will try it.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Store count of app-first chains in the city: 2 in June 2025, 22 by 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Luckin Coffee opened its first two US stores in Greenwich Village and Chelsea in June 2025 with $1.99 opening drinks and had 22 New York stores within about a year, some in former Starbucks sites
eventCatalog.note: 5% for the three months of opening coupons is my estimate; the effect is strongest on students and weakest on regulars.

eventCatalog.name: A 500-square-foot rival opens next door
eventCatalog.text: A venture-backed chain fits a counter, an automatic machine and two staff into a space a third of yours. Its rent per cup is lower than yours.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Small-format chain store counts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Blank Street: 106 stores worldwide by August 2026 after a $105 million funding round; stores of about 500 sq ft with automatic espresso machines and two or three staff; matcha is about half of its sales
eventCatalog.note: What the rival cannot offer is seats and a reason to stay; the moves listed are the ones that sell that. 5% is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: The chain store on the block closes
eventCatalog.text: The chain did not renew. A few hundred people a day need a new morning stop.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain closures: Starbucks closed 42 New York stores in 2025
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Chains in New York City shrank 1.3% in 2025 (112 stores), the sixth decline in eight years; 18 chains left the city entirely
eventCatalog.note: The gain is real only if the shop can serve it: chain customers expect phone ordering and a four-minute wait. 6% is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: The cafe across the street closes
eventCatalog.text: Its regulars are loyal to their order, not to the room. Some will try you this week.
eventCatalog.realSignal: A rival's bankruptcy or closure on the same block (in the game: another player or a resident business)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Follows from the game itself: the engine already hands half of turned-away buyers to neighbors
eventCatalog.note: 4% is my estimate; the engine's own split of the block's passers-by may already produce it, in which case this entry is only the announcement text.

eventCatalog.name: A coffee cart sets up by the subway stairs
eventCatalog.text: A licensed cart sells drip coffee and a roll for about half your price, exactly where commuters surface.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Mobile food vending permits issued by the Health Department: 2,200 more supervisory license applications a year from 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 6,880 food vendor permits before the 2026 reform; a waiting list of more than 10,000
eventCatalog.note: See events coffee_cart_at_the_stairs.

eventCatalog.name: The big employer nearby orders five days in the office
eventCatalog.text: From next month the tower around the corner fills on Mondays and Fridays too.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Return-to-office announcements; Kastle and Placer.ai office indexes
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Placer.ai: mandates are usually announced for September or January. Partnership for New York City, March 2025: one employer in four planned to require more office days
eventCatalog.note: Applies to blocks with an office anchor. 6% is the place model's weekday commuter effect, an assumption there too.

eventCatalog.name: The office building next door is being converted to apartments
eventCatalog.text: The tenants are gone and the scaffolding is up. For a year or two nobody works or lives there; after that, a thousand neighbors.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Department of Buildings conversion filings; the Comptroller's office-to-residential tracker
eventCatalog.realFrequency: More than 15 million sq ft of office conversions under way in New York, about 16,000-17,400 apartments; another 9.5-9.8 million sq ft planned to start in 2026; Midtown has passed the Financial District
eventCatalog.note: 10% during construction is my estimate for a shop that drew a fifth of its orders from that building. When the apartments fill, the week shape turns from 'office' to 'neighborhood' (extra.weekdayProfiles).

eventCatalog.name: A new apartment building opens on the block
eventCatalog.text: Several hundred new neighbors arrive within a few months, and none of them has a coffee habit here yet.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Certificates of occupancy for new residential buildings
eventCatalog.realFrequency: See office_tower_becomes_apartments
eventCatalog.note: 4% is my estimate. New residents choose a regular cafe in their first weeks; the shop that is open on their first Saturday keeps them.

eventCatalog.name: The semester starts
eventCatalog.text: Thousands of students are back and looking for their place for the year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: University calendars: NYU fall classes start September 2, 2026; spring classes January 19, 2027
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Twice a year. CUNY about 247,000 students, NYU about 56,800, Columbia about 35,200
eventCatalog.note: 6% is the place model's in-term effect near a college, an assumption there. Students are the most price-sensitive group and the heaviest users of seats.

eventCatalog.name: Finals week: every seat taken by 10am
eventCatalog.text: Students camp for six hours on one drink. Walk-in customers look at the full room and keep walking.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Exam weeks: NYU December 16-22, 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Twice a year, one to two weeks each
eventCatalog.note: Seat turnover is not an event target yet (requests). Sizes are my estimates: a quarter fewer sit-down orders per seat, slightly more people at the door.

eventCatalog.name: Campus empties for the summer
eventCatalog.text: Classes ended and the dorms cleared out. The block is quiet until September.
eventCatalog.realSignal: University calendars
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year, mid-May to early September
eventCatalog.note: 12% is the place model's summer effect near a college (keen-cray branch), an assumption there. See events campus_summer_break for the mixed-block version.

eventCatalog.name: A food creator films your block
eventCatalog.text: A video about 'the best coffee street downtown' passes a million views. Saturday's line goes around the corner, at every cafe on the block.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Views of videos tagged with the neighborhood; map searches for the block
eventCatalog.realFrequency: No rate. Cases: a Williamsburg cafe whose owner's video passed six million views had lines down the block and cut the line off at 3pm; a Manhattan luncheonette had two-to-three-hour waits for months after one video and 'wasn't ready'
eventCatalog.note: Announced to the whole block, so it is not luck for one player. The catch is capacity: a shop that cannot serve the surge loses orders and collects 'slow' reviews (slow_service_reviews). 25% for a month is my estimate; the cases suggest it can be far more.

eventCatalog.name: Everyone is back after Labor Day
eventCatalog.text: Schools open, vacations end and the offices fill in the same week. The strongest stretch of the year begins.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Kastle weekly occupancy; MTA daily ridership (records in September and October 2026)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. 2026: 4,696,692 subway rides on Wednesday September 23 and 4.72 million on Thursday October 29, the highest since the pandemic; Kastle's New York peak of the year was Tuesday October 27 at 87.3%
eventCatalog.note: 5% is extra.monthCurve's September-October level against the year's average.

eventCatalog.name: Summer Fridays
eventCatalog.text: From late July to Labor Day the offices run half empty, most of all on Fridays.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Placer.ai monthly office index; Kastle weekly occupancy; the Friday share of office visits
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. Fridays hold 11.9% of New York's office visits (first half of 2026) against 12.4% nationally in 2025
eventCatalog.note: 8% is for an office-district block (extra.monthCurve.office July-August against average); the mixed-block version is events summer_friday_slump.

eventCatalog.name: Offices empty out for the holidays
eventCatalog.text: From Thanksgiving week to the first days of January the towers thin out.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Placer.ai December office index: 33.1% under 2019 in December 2025
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year: the week of Thanksgiving and the last two weeks of December
eventCatalog.note: 15% over a month is for an office-district block: two near-empty weeks out of four. Tourist corridors gain in the same weeks.

eventCatalog.name: January slump
eventCatalog.text: Resolutions, cold mornings and half-empty offices. Owners say customers disappear at the start of every year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Census monthly food service sales, not seasonally adjusted; the shop's own January against December
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year
eventCatalog.note: See events january_slump.

eventCatalog.name: Autumn drink season
eventCatalog.text: The chains launch their autumn drinks in late August. Customers expect something seasonal from you too.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain launch dates; Placer.ai visit counts on launch days
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year
eventCatalog.note: Should apply to shops running the seasonal drink; shops without one get 0.99. See events autumn_drink_season.

eventCatalog.name: Holiday cups arrive
eventCatalog.text: Red cups and peppermint everything. The chains' launch day is one of their busiest of the year.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Placer.ai: Starbucks visits 44.5% above average on its November 2025 launch day
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year
eventCatalog.note: 2% for an independent with a seasonal drink is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: National Coffee Day: the chains give coffee away
eventCatalog.text: On September 29 half the chains hand out a free or 25-cent coffee through their apps. For one day your drip coffee competes with free.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The chains' published offers for September 29
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. 2026: Dunkin' free medium coffee with a purchase for app members; Tim Hortons and Circle K free coffee; Peet's a 25-cent drip
eventCatalog.note: One day out of thirty: a 15% dip that day is 0.5% of the month, my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: Peak visitor season
eventCatalog.text: Hotels are close to full. Visitors choose a cafe on the map: the stars and the photos do the selling.
eventCatalog.realSignal: CoStar monthly hotel occupancy for New York City; NYC Tourism visitor counts
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Occupancy 87.9% in May 2025, 86.6% in September, 89.4% in October
eventCatalog.note: 8% is for a tourist corridor; events tourist_high_season carries the mixed-block version.

eventCatalog.name: The tourists are gone
eventCatalog.text: January and February are the quietest weeks of the year for visitors.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Monthly hotel occupancy
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Every year. The January and February occupancy figures were not found in this session
eventCatalog.note: 12% is extra.monthCurve.tourist for January-February against the average month, my estimate; the winter hotel numbers behind it were not seen.

eventCatalog.name: Fewer visitors from abroad
eventCatalog.text: International arrivals fell while domestic trips held. Shops on the tourist streets feel it; side streets do not.
eventCatalog.realSignal: NYC Tourism: international visitors 12.5 million in 2025, down 3.2%
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 2025: total visitors 65 million (+0.7%), international 12.5 million (-3.2%). Forecast for 2026: 66.3 million, international 12.9 million
eventCatalog.note: 2% applies to tourist corridors only; international visitors stay longer and spend more per head than domestic ones.

eventCatalog.name: World Cup summer
eventCatalog.text: World Cup matches across the river. Fans fill the bars that show the games; streets near fan zones are packed or closed.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Match schedule June 11 - July 19, 2026; card transaction volumes
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Once. Restaurant transactions in New York and New Jersey +18.5% in the group stage; venues showing matches +63% sales; one restaurant by the stadium -60% on match days
eventCatalog.note: See events world_cup_summer.

eventCatalog.name: Delivery keeps growing
eventCatalog.text: More app orders every year, even with higher courier pay.
eventCatalog.realSignal: The city's delivery app reports: orders per week
eventCatalog.realFrequency: 3.3 million orders a week in June 2026 against 2.6 million in December 2023
eventCatalog.note: See events delivery_orders_keep_growing.

eventCatalog.name: The city reopens the delivery fee caps
eventCatalog.text: The consumer agency is asking whether the caps on app fees are too high or too low. Whatever it recommends lands on your commission.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Department of Consumer and Worker Protection fee-cap review (required every two years) and its rule notices
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Caps set in 2020, made permanent by Local Law 103 of 2021, loosened by Local Law 79 of 2025 (enhanced services up to 20%); a feedback round ran in April 2026 and a recordkeeping rule was proposed in mid-2026. In April 2026 the city won more than $580,000 in refunds for over 380 restaurants from one app
eventCatalog.note: The direction and size of the next change are unknown; 10% more commission is a placeholder for 'the terms move'. deliveryCommission is not an event target yet (requests).

eventCatalog.name: Customers trade down
eventCatalog.text: Households cut small luxuries first. Quick-service visits are falling and a $7 latte is easy to skip.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Placer.ai quick-service visits year over year; Starbucks comparable transactions; University of Michigan consumer sentiment
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Quick-service visits -1.3% in January-July 2026 and -4.5% in May 2026 year over year; Starbucks US transactions -10% in its fourth fiscal quarter of 2024
eventCatalog.note: See events consumers_trade_down. The consumer sentiment reading for autumn 2026 was not found.

eventCatalog.name: Everyone's prices creep up
eventCatalog.text: Coffee shop prices rise about 4% a year. A shop that never moves its prices gets cheaper against the street every month, and gives away margin.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Toast's median menu prices; Bureau of Labor Statistics index of food away from home
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Median drip coffee $3.65 in February 2026 (+4.3% in a year); median cold brew $5.75 in October 2026 (+4.0%)
eventCatalog.note: fairPrice (the engine's reference price) is not an event target yet (requests). Without it the reference price stays at $8.50 for the whole year while real customers' sense of a fair price moves.

eventCatalog.name: The chain's baristas walk out
eventCatalog.text: Picket lines at the chain's unionized stores. Some of its customers will not cross them and look for coffee nearby.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Strike announcements by the union; list of struck stores
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks Workers United struck from the company's 'Red Cup Day' in November 2025 with more than 1,000 workers, New York stores among them; the city's mayor-elect joined a picket in December 2025; in August 2026 the union called for a nationwide boycott
eventCatalog.note: Applies within 250 m of a struck store. No measurement of customers moving to independents was found; 3% is my estimate. The same customers ask how you treat your own staff.

eventCatalog.name: The chain's restrooms are now for customers only
eventCatalog.text: The chain down the street stopped letting everyone in. The people it turns away now ask at your counter.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain policy announcements
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks reversed its seven-year open-door policy in January 2025
eventCatalog.note: cleaningCost is not an event target (requests); 15% more cleaning for an open restroom is my estimate. A shop with fewer than 20 seats has no duty to offer one.

eventCatalog.name: Weekends come back faster than weekdays
eventCatalog.text: The city's weekends are almost as busy as before the pandemic; its weekdays are not. Neighborhood shops gain, office-district shops wait.
eventCatalog.realSignal: MTA ridership against 2019: weekdays and weekends separately
eventCatalog.realFrequency: State Comptroller, April 2026: weekend subway ridership was 89% of 2019 in 2025 (80% in 2024); weekday ridership 74% (68% in 2024)
eventCatalog.note: 3% a year on weekend days for residential blocks is my estimate from the 9-point gain in weekend ridership.

eventCatalog.name: More commuters every year
eventCatalog.text: Weekday ridership sets a new post-pandemic record. Shops at the stairs see it first, between 7 and 9.
eventCatalog.realSignal: MTA weekday ridership: 68% of 2019 in 2024, 74% in 2025, record days in autumn 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Thursday October 29, 2026: 4.72 million rides, 9.7% more than the same day a year earlier
eventCatalog.note: 4% a year for blocks with a subway anchor is my estimate: weekday ridership rose 6 points on a base of 68 (+9%), and not every rider is a new customer.

eventCatalog.name: Everyone wants matcha
eventCatalog.text: Green drinks outsell espresso at the newest chains. Customers ask for them by name, mostly in the afternoon.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Menu mix of fast-growing chains; search interest
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Matcha is about half of Blank Street's sales (2026)
eventCatalog.note: Applies to shops with the wide menu or a seasonal drink; 3% is my estimate. Task D04 owns the ingredient cost.

eventCatalog.name: Regulators go after fake reviews
eventCatalog.text: Warning letters went out to companies with suspicious reviews. Platforms purge and label.
eventCatalog.realSignal: FTC enforcement announcements under the review rule
eventCatalog.realFrequency: The rule took effect on October 21, 2024; the first ten warning letters went out in December 2025
eventCatalog.note: The move here is to stop a shortcut: the event raises the chance that an open fake_reviews trail is checked. 30% more checks is a game value.

eventCatalog.name: The city sweeps for hidden fees
eventCatalog.text: Consumer inspectors are checking receipts against posted prices across the neighborhood.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Consumer protection enforcement announcements; the restaurant surcharge rule amended in 2026
eventCatalog.realFrequency: One restaurant in five now adds some extra fee (National Restaurant Association), up from 16% in 2022; the city adopted amendments to its restaurant surcharge rule in March 2026
eventCatalog.note: A game value for the size. The lawful alternative is the card_pricing lever.

eventCatalog.name: The catering marketplace gets a new owner
eventCatalog.text: A delivery giant is buying the site office managers use to order breakfast. More orders may come; the commission may change.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Merger announcements; the marketplace's fee page
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Uber agreed to buy ezCater in October 2026; current fees are 15% + 2.99%
eventCatalog.note: Applies only to shops with the catering lever on. 1% is my estimate.

eventCatalog.name: A chain caps its 'unlimited' coffee pass
eventCatalog.text: After four years the best-known coffee subscription stopped being unlimited: 30 drinks a month. Heavy users were drinking the margin.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Subscription terms of the large chains
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Panera's pass launched in 2022 at $10.99 a month, cost $14.99 by 2026 and was capped at 30 drinks from August 19, 2026
eventCatalog.note: A lesson more than a shock: a pass must have a cap. 1% is my estimate of displaced pass holders looking for another routine.

eventCatalog.name: The chains go after the afternoon
eventCatalog.text: More than half of a big chain's sales happen before 11am, so it now pushes iced, low-caffeine and energy drinks after lunch. The quiet hours are where the next fight is.
eventCatalog.realSignal: Chain menu launches for the afternoon; share of chain visits between 3 and 7pm (Starbucks 23.7%, Dunkin' 16.4% in 2024)
eventCatalog.realFrequency: Starbucks, 2026: digital menu boards that switch to afternoon items; iced fruit drinks grew at double-digit rates; record food sales with the largest gains in the afternoon
eventCatalog.note: 1% of the day is my estimate of what an independent with no afternoon offer gives up; a shop with the wide menu or a seasonal drink should gain the same amount instead. The afternoon hours are where a neighborhood cafe has spare bar capacity.
